blocks.text: Long ago, in the land of the Sakyas, there lived a young prince called Siddhartha. His father was King Suddhodana.

One day the prince wanted to go to his pleasure garden, so he told his charioteer to get his chariot ready. The charioteer harnessed four splendid horses, as white as lotus flowers, and the prince set off for the garden.

Now the gods thought, "The time is coming when Prince Siddhartha will become a Buddha. Let us show him the signs." So one of the gods took the shape of a very old man, with grey hair and broken teeth, bent over and leaning on a stick. Only the prince and his charioteer could see him.
"What kind of man is that?" asked the prince. "Even his hair is not like other men's."
The charioteer told him that the man was old.
"Then shame on life," said the prince, "if everyone who is born must grow old!" His heart was troubled, and he turned back at once and went home to the palace.
"Why has my son come back so soon?" asked the king.
"He has seen an old man," they told him. "And now that he has seen an old man, he will leave the world."

"You will ruin me!" cried the king. "Quick, have music and plays put on for my son. As long as he is enjoying himself, he won't think of leaving the world!" And he put more guards all around the palace, half a league away on every side.

Another day, as the prince was going to his garden, the gods showed him a sick man. He asked the same question as before, and his heart was troubled, and he turned back home. And the king did as he had done before, and put his guards farther out, three-quarters of a league away.
Another day, the gods showed the prince a dead man. Again his heart was troubled, and he turned back home. And the king put his guards still farther out, a whole league away.
Then, one more day, the gods showed the prince a man who had given up everything he owned, quietly and neatly dressed. "Friend," the prince asked his charioteer, "what kind of man is that?"

In those days there was no Buddha in the world, so the charioteer did not know what such a man was. But the gods put the words into his mouth. "That is a holy man who has left the world," he said, and he told the prince how good it is to give up the world. That day the prince went on to his pleasure garden, thinking about leaving the world himself.

All day he enjoyed himself in the garden, and bathed in the lovely lake. At sunset he sat down on the royal stone to be dressed, and his servants stood around him with robes of many colours, and jewels, and garlands, and perfumes.

Just then, far away in heaven, the throne of Sakka, the king of the gods, grew warm. Sakka saw why, and he said to the god Vissakamma, "Tonight at midnight, Prince Siddhartha will leave the world. This is the last time he will be dressed in splendour. Go to the garden and dress him in heavenly clothes."

So Vissakamma took the shape of the royal barber, and wound the turban around the prince's head, and the jewels in it shone in a thousand folds. At his touch the prince knew, "This is no man. This is a god." Then, while the musicians played and the people cheered, he climbed into his chariot.
At that moment a message came from the king. The prince's wife had given birth to a baby son. "Tell my son how happy I am!" the king said.

When the prince heard the news, he said, "Something has been born to hold me back. Something has been born to tie me down." And when the king heard what he had said, he said, "Then let my grandson's name be Rahula," which means "something that holds you back".

Then the prince rode back into the city in great splendour. A young noblewoman called Kisa Gotami was standing on the flat roof of her house, and when she saw how beautiful and noble the prince looked, she was filled with joy, and she sang:

Happy is the mother,
happy is the father,
happy is the wife
of such a glorious lord!

The prince heard her, and thought, "She says that the heart of a mother is made happy, and of a father, and of a wife. But what can make every heart happy, and at peace, for ever?" And the answer came to him: "When the fires of greed and hatred and foolishness have gone out, then there is peace. That is what I have been looking for. This very day I will leave home, and look for that peace!"

He took off his pearl necklace, which was worth a hundred thousand pieces of money, and sent it to Kisa Gotami, to thank her for her lesson. She was delighted. "Prince Siddhartha must have fallen in love with me," she thought. But the prince went into his palace and lay down on his couch.

Then lovely dancers and singers came with their instruments, and danced, and sang, and played for him. But the prince took no pleasure in it, and he fell asleep. "The prince we were playing for has gone to sleep," said the dancers. "Why should we go on?" So they put down their instruments, and lay down and went to sleep too.

The prince woke up. The lamps were burning low, and he saw the dancers lying asleep all over the floor, some yawning, some muttering in their sleep, some with their mouths wide open, and their fine clothes all crumpled. The beautiful hall did not look beautiful to him any more. Now the whole world of pleasures seemed to him like a house on fire. "I can't bear it!" he cried, and he made up his mind to leave that very night.
He got up, went to the door, and called, "Who is there?"
"It is I, sir, Channa," said his servant, who was sleeping with his head on the doorstep.
"I am leaving the world tonight," said the prince. "Saddle me a horse."

Channa went to the stables, and there by the light of the lamps he saw the great horse Kanthaka. "This is the one I should saddle tonight," he thought. As Channa saddled him, Kanthaka knew, "My master is leaving the world tonight." He was so glad that he gave a mighty neigh, which would have woken the whole town, but the gods stopped the sound so that no one heard it.

Meanwhile the prince thought, "I will just look at my son." He went to his wife's room and opened the door. A sweet-smelling lamp was burning dimly. His wife lay asleep on a bed strewn with jasmine flowers, with her hand on the baby's head. The prince stopped in the doorway. "If I move her hand to pick up my son, she will wake up, and then I will never be able to go," he thought. "I will come back and see him when I have become a Buddha." And he left the palace.

He went to Kanthaka. "My good Kanthaka," he said, "carry me just this one night, so that when I have become a Buddha, I can save the world of people and the world of the gods too." And he leaped up onto the horse's back.

Kanthaka was huge, strong and swift, and as white as a clean seashell. The gods muffled the sound of his neighing, and put their hands under his hooves at every step so that no one would hear. The prince rode on, with Channa holding on to the horse's tail, and at midnight they came to the great gate of the city.

The king had put a thousand men at each gate, to stop the prince from leaving. But the prince thought, "If the gate does not open, I will jump Kanthaka right over the wall." Channa thought, "If the gate does not open, I will carry my master on my shoulders, and hold Kanthaka tight under my arm, and jump over the wall." And Kanthaka thought, "If the gate does not open, I will jump over the wall with my master on my back and Channa holding my tail." But the spirit who lived in the gate opened it for them.
At that moment Mara, the Tempter, came to stop the prince. He stood in the air and called out, "Do not go, my lord! In seven days you will become the emperor of the whole world. Stay, my lord!"
"Who are you?" said the prince.
"I am Vasavatti," came the answer.
"Mara!" said the prince. "I know very well that I could rule the world. But it is not a kingdom that I want. I will become a Buddha, and make the whole universe shout for joy."

Then Mara thought, "From now on, whenever a greedy or angry or unkind thought comes into your mind, I will know it." And he followed the prince everywhere, as close as his own shadow, watching for him to slip.

So the prince left the city, on the night of the full moon. As he went, he wanted to look back at the city once more, and at that moment the whole earth turned round like a potter's wheel, so that he could see it without stopping. Then he rode on. The gods carried thousands of torches all around him, and flowers fell from the sky like rain, and heavenly music filled the air.
In that one night he passed through three kingdoms and came to a river. "What is this river called?" he asked Channa.
"It is called Anoma, my lord," said Channa. Anoma means "noble".

"Then my leaving the world shall be called Anoma too," said the prince. And at a touch of his heel, Kanthaka leaped right across the river, which was five or six hundred yards wide, and landed on the other side.

The prince got down from the horse and stood on the sandy bank, which shone like a sheet of silver. "Good Channa," he said, "go home now, and take my jewels and Kanthaka with you. I am going to become a holy man."
"Then I will become a holy man too, my lord," said Channa.
"No, you must go back," said the prince. Three times Channa asked, and three times the prince said no. And he gave Channa his jewels and his horse.

Then the prince thought, "This long hair is not right for a holy man." So he took his sword in his right hand, and with his left hand he held his long hair and his jewelled turban, and he cut them off. His hair was left just two inches long, curling close to his head, and it stayed that way all his life.

"If I am to become a Buddha," he said, "let this hair stay up in the air. If not, let it fall to the ground." And he threw his hair and the turban up towards the sky. Up they went, a whole league high, and stopped there in the air. And Sakka, the king of the gods, saw them, and caught them in a jewelled casket, and took them up to heaven.

Then the prince thought, "These fine clothes are not right for a holy man." Now, long ago, in an earlier life, he had had a friend who was now a god, called Ghatikara. And Ghatikara thought, "Today my friend is leaving the world. I will bring him what a holy man needs." So he brought the prince the eight things that a holy man may own:

Three robes, and a bowl for begging,
a razor, a needle, a belt,
and a strainer for water: these eight
are all the riches of a holy man.
So the prince put on the simple robes of a holy man. He told Channa to go home and tell his father and mother that he was safe. And Channa bowed to him with great respect, and went away.

A simplified retelling of “The Four Omens and the Great Renunciation” in Buddhist Birth Stories, translated by T. W. Rhys Davids (1880). The original is listed under Other versions. Rhys Davids writes the prince's name in its Pāli form, Siddhattha. Sakka is the king of the gods, and Mara is the Tempter. A holy man who has left the world owns nothing, and begs for his food.
